title: The Fox Wedding on the Bridge

pages.text:
*The Owl Alley Sheet, No. 2. Today's news: foxes were not seen at any wedding.*

The voice was round and loud, bouncing off the wooden walls of Owl Alley.

"The foxes danced! The foxes danced on Willow Bridge!"

Bunta stood in the street, his deep straw hat pulled low over his eyes. He waved a paper sheet high above his head. Around him, a crowd had gathered. There were women with baskets, men with tools, and one very large cat who watched with unblinking interest.

Haru squeezed through the legs of the people to get a better look. Bunta’s voice rose like steam from a pot. "Lanterns! Silk robes! A wedding of spirits! All true!"

Beside him stood Gohei, thin as a reed. He did not wave. He did not shout. He watched the street corners. He watched the alley behind the tofu shop. He watched for men in dark coats, the magistrate’s men, who did not like unlicensed news.

"Why the hats?" Haru whispered to Mother Okiyo, who was leaning out the shop door.

"Privacy," Mother said, smiling. "And pairs. Two are harder to ignore than one. But harder to catch, too."

Bunta turned the paper over. The ink was still wet. It smelled of pine soot and ambition.
pages.image: A round seller in a deep straw hat and indigo striped kimono waves a blank paper sheet loudly to a small crowd in a narrow wooden alley, while a thin seller in a brown kimono watches the street corner nervously beside him, with a large cat sitting in the foreground.

pages.text:
Haru dug into her sleeve and found a small copper coin that felt heavy and cold. She had saved it for three weeks, turning it over in her palm until the edges felt smooth. She pressed it into Bunta’s hand, and he handed her the sheet, which was thick paper that felt expensive.

Haru looked down. The picture was beautiful. Two foxes sat on a bridge, wearing tiny, intricate robes with lanterns hanging from their paws. The carving was fine, the lines crisp, and the foxes looked soft and proud. It was not just news; it was art.

Haru felt a hot prick in her chest. She wanted to be angry at the lies, and she wanted to be angry at the sellers, but mostly she was angry that it was so well made. Her father’s blocks were honest and sturdy, but they did not make her heart stutter. She tucked the sheet into her apron, and the paper rustled against her hip like a soft, dry whisper.
pages.image: Haru, an eleven-year-old girl in a rust-orange kimono and indigo apron, holds a blank paper sheet with both hands, looking down at it with a serious expression, her fingers slightly curled around the edges, standing in the crowded wooden alley with other customers blurred in the background.

pages.text:
Later, at the carving table, Master Sota was slicing a cherry-wood block, the knife making a soft scraping sound against the grain.

"Did you see it?" he asked without looking up.

"Did I see the foxes?" Haru asked.

He nodded, the wood shaving curling away from the edge.

"No," Haru said. "I crossed Willow Bridge last night on the way home from the bathhouse. It was foggy. I saw one cat that looked confused, and two broken lanterns hanging from a fence. I saw fog. I saw cold."

Master Sota set his knife down and wiped his hands on his cloth, the motion slow and deliberate.

"Most people know a story when they see one," he said quietly. "They buy it because it is warm. They do not check the wood grain."

"Not everyone," Haru said, her voice sharp as a chip. She tapped her brush against her teeth. "Some people need to be told. Some people think the bridge is actually made of foxes."

Master Sota looked at her, his eyes steady and calm. He picked up his knife again, the blade catching the light from the window.

"Then we must tell them," he said. "But tell them true."
pages.image: Father Sota, a broad calm man in a dark brown work coat and white headband, sits at a low wooden table holding a carving knife, looking up at Haru, who stands beside him in her rust-orange kimono, tapping a small brush against her teeth, with shelves of wooden blocks visible behind them.

pages.text:
The door curtain slid aside, and Jiro stepped out onto the stone step of the Turtle House. He was twelve, neat and proud, wearing a bright yellow silk kimono with a black diamond pattern. His hair was tied in a small topknot, and he fanned himself with a silk handkerchief, though the air was biting.

"Haru," he said, his voice light. "How did your sheet sell?"

Kichi, who was drying his hands on a towel, leaned over the counter. "Eleven," he said. "We had eleven buyers. Jiro, did you sell more?"

"By noon, we were out," Jiro replied. He smiled, a thin, proud expression. "The foxes are very popular. They are polite, too. They never complain about the ink."

Kichi grinned. "That is good. Foxes make excellent proofreaders. They catch every smudge."

Jiro’s smile did not waver. He looked at Haru. She did not smile back, but her eyes stayed fixed on his bright yellow sleeve.

"Eleven is a lot for a lie," Haru said.

Jiro’s fan stopped moving. He tucked it neatly into his obi. "Eleven is a lot for a truth," he said. "It depends on who is listening."
pages.image: Jiro, a twelve-year-old boy in a bright yellow silk kimono with a black diamond pattern and tall wooden geta, stands on a stone step fanning himself with a white handkerchief, looking at Haru, who stands near the shop counter in her rust-orange kimono, while Kichi in a moss-green coat watches from behind the counter.

pages.text:
That night, Haru lay in the sleeping loft. The wood creaked above her. Below, she could hear the shop settling into sleep. The smell of dried ink and cherry wood curled around her.

She held the fox sheet in her hands. The paper was smooth. The foxes looked up at her from the dark.

Grandfather Tobei had come up to check on her. He sat on the edge of the loft, his bad shoulder rubbing against the wood.

"A fast paper runs," he said. His voice was low and dry. "It moves quickly. It sells well. But it leaves no footprint."

Haru looked at the blank sheet in her hand.

"A true paper lasts," he continued. "It sits on a table. It is read again. It does not run. It stays."

He stood up, his wooden stick tapping the floor.

"The question, Haru, is not whether you have the truth. You have it. The question is whether you have the hand to hold it steady."

He left her in the dark. She turned the fox sheet over. The back was blank. She thought about what it would take to fill it with something that stayed.
pages.image: Haru, an eleven-year-old girl in a rust-orange kimono, sits up on a thin folded quilt on a plain wooden loft floor, holding a blank paper sheet, no bed and no pillow, while Grandfather Tobei, a thin old man with a white topknot and blue-grey kimono, stands nearby leaning on a wooden stick, looking down at her with a calm expression.
